aspects.title: Inline links distinguished from body text by hue alone (no underline/weight/lightness), incl. hover/focus-only cues that don't rescue
aspects.description: Links embedded in running text have their underline removed and are set in a color that differs from the surrounding body text by HUE only — there is no bold, italic, size, font-family change, and the link-vs-text lightness contrast is under 3:1. A sighted color-perceiving user can spot the links; a color-blind or grayscale user cannot tell them apart from prose. To flag this an evaluator must (a) recognize which colored spans are actually links (vs decorative emphasis) by reading the markup/meaning, (b) confirm hue is the ONLY differentiator, and (c) judge that any subtle non-color cue present (a faint weight bump, a serif/sans swap) is too weak to count. A critical sub-case: the only non-color cue is injected on :hover or :focus — F73 and G183 are explicit that a cue appearing only on hover/focus is STILL a failure because the resting state is color-only; detecting this requires comparing the resting render to the hover/focus render and applying the rule. This is the canonical 'distinguishing a visual element' failure and is the single most prevalent real-world 1.4.1 defect.
aspects.scLimb: distinguishing a visual element (LIMB 4) + scoping: hover/focus cues do not rescue + 3:1 lightness escape hatch
aspects.whyUncovered:
There are 0 ACT rules and 0 test cases for 1.4.1, so this is entirely unexercised. axe/Lighthouse/WAVE have NO link-vs-surrounding-text contrast rule — their contrast checks measure foreground-vs-background per 1.4.3, not link-color-vs-adjacent-TEXT-color, and they treat an un-underlined colored inside

as fine. Deciding whether a colored span is a real link vs decorative emphasis, whether a subtle non-color cue is 'enough', and whether a hover/focus-only cue rescues the resting state are all perceptual/contextual judgments no automated checker performs.

references.quote: Removing the underline and leaving only the color difference for such links would be a failure because there would be no other visual indication (besides color) that it is a link.
If the non-color cue only happens when the mouse hovers over the link or when the link receives focus, it is still a failure.

Red and pink are the same color (hue) but they have different lightness (which is not color). So red and pink would pass the requirement for "not distinguished by color (hue) alone" since they differ by lightness (which is not color) - as long as the difference in lightness (contrast) is 3:1 or greater.
Hover or focus style changes alone are not sufficient to meet the criterion.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained HTML paragraphs with mixed inline <a> links. Vary the failing mechanism per page: (1) un-underlined blue links at <3:1 link-vs-text lightness; (2) gray-on-gray same-hue at ~2:1; (3) the literal F73 hover-only underline; (4) :focus-visible-only bold weight; (5) a same-lightness colored-emphasis decoy where some colored words are links and some are not. Include at least one TRUE-NEGATIVE page (links pass on >=3:1 lightness with no other cue, OR a hyperlink styled identically to static text conveying no actionable distinction) to exercise the escape-hatch / non-applicability boundaries — an over-eager tool would wrongly flag these. To verify hover/focus cases the evaluator must capture and compare resting vs hover/focus screenshots.
suggestedScenarios: Blog paragraph with three inline <a> links styled #2a5db0 with text-decoration:none on black body text (link-vs-text contrast ~2.5:1) — links vanish in grayscale.
'Further reading' paragraph where link text is a slightly darker shade of the SAME gray hue as body text at ~2:1 lightness with no other cue.
Literal F73 example: a:link/a:visited/a:active have no underline, a:hover adds underline+red — must be judged in resting state to fail.
Inline links color-only at rest that gain bold weight only on :focus-visible — keyboard-discoverable but resting mouse-state is color-only.
Paragraph mixing colored-bold link words and colored-bold NON-link emphasis words in the same hue, so only href-reading reveals which are clickable.
TRUE-NEGATIVE: links light-blue (#3366CC) on black at 3.9:1 lightness with no underline — should PASS via the 3:1 escape hatch.

TRUE-NEGATIVE (non-applicability): a hyperlink styled to look exactly like neighboring static text (same color, no underline) — does NOT fail 1.4.1 because no color differentiation conveys the link-ness.

aspects.title: Required form fields indicated by color alone, with self-referential or absent text instruction
aspects.description: A form marks required fields by coloring their labels (e.g. red) or adding a colored border, with NO asterisk, no '(required)', no icon, and no per-field text cue. The trap that demands human judgment: there may be a general instruction at the top, but it is itself color-keyed ('Required fields are shown in red') — which is useless to someone who cannot perceive red, since it never lets them identify WHICH specific fields are required. An evaluator must (1) see that color is the only visual distinction between required and optional labels, (2) confirm no per-field non-color cue exists, and (3) judge whether any general instruction genuinely RESOLVES which fields are required for a color-blind user, rather than merely mentioning the color rule. 'Required fields are red' passes a literal text-present check yet still fails because the alternative is self-referentially color-dependent.
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases for 1.4.1. Checkers may detect a missing required attribute (a separate 1.3.1/3.3.x concern that does NOT satisfy 1.4.1's VISIBLE-alternative requirement), but no automated rule judges whether the visible required-vs-optional distinction is color-only, nor whether a prose instruction effectively resolves the ambiguity for a color-blind user. The self-referential-instruction failure ('required fields are red' is itself color-keyed) is a pure semantic judgment.

references.quote: To indicate that the phone number field is required, the label "Phone Number" is displayed in a color different from the color used for optional fields, without any other indication that "Phone Number" is a required field. A person with color vision deficiency or low vision may not be able to identify that "Phone Number" is a required field.
The instructions for an online form say, "Required fields are shown in red and marked with (required)." The cue "(required)" is included within the label element.
Examples of information conveyed by color differences: “required fields are red", “error is shown in red", and “Mary's sales are in red, Tom's are in blue".

It would also not fail if the color chosen had sufficient luminosity difference (lightness) from the other text that it would be easily be seen as different if viewed in black and white. A minimum contrast ratio of 3:1 is considered sufficient.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained forms with mixed required/optional fields. Vary the cue location and trap: (1) red labels, black optional labels, only instruction is 'Required fields appear in red'; (2) red left-border on the input with no text cue; (3) layered trap where a red asterisk is itself distinguishable from a decorative red bullet only by color. Include TRUE-NEGATIVE pages: red labels PLUS '(required)' per G205, and a green-vs-gray label distinction at >3:1 lightness that should PASS via the escape hatch — to confirm the evaluator applies the lightness rule instead of reflexively failing any color cue. A mixed-section form (some sections asterisked, some red-only) forces per-field rather than global judgment.
suggestedScenarios: Registration form: required labels red, optional black, no asterisk/icon, instruction reads only 'Required fields appear in red' (self-referential color-keyed instruction).
Form where required fields get a red left-border on the <input> (not the label) with no text cue — the border color is the sole signal.
Layered trap: required cue is a red label PLUS a red asterisk that is only distinguishable from a decorative red bullet by color.
Multi-section form where only some sections' required fields are red-only while others use '(required)' text — forces per-field judgment, no global verdict.
TRUE-NEGATIVE: red required labels PLUS '(required)' inside each <label> and an at-top legend (G205 endorsed) — should PASS.
TRUE-NEGATIVE: required cue is a label whose color differs from optional by >3:1 lightness (green vs gray) — should PASS via the lightness escape hatch.

aspects.title: Error / validation feedback conveyed by color alone (red border or red text only) in the post-submit state
aspects.description: After a failed submit (or during inline validation), fields that failed are outlined or tinted red, or have their label turned red, with NO error icon, NO inline error message, and NO '(error)' marker — the only signal that THIS field is wrong is its hue. Per F81 and Trusted Tester, an error indicator cannot use color alone. An evaluator must reach/observe the dynamic post-validation state, notice the erroring field is distinguished from valid fields purely by color, and confirm no adjacent non-color error cue exists. This is the 'prompting a response' limb (highlighting a field to prompt correction). Crucially, programmatic exposure via aria-invalid does NOT satisfy 1.4.1, which requires a VISIBLE alternative for sighted color-blind users who are not using AT.
aspects.scLimb: prompting a response (LIMB 3) — 'error is shown in red' / highlighting a field that needs correction; AT-decoupling note
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases for 1.4.1. The error state is dynamic (appears after a failed submit), beyond static-page scanners. Even with the state rendered, no automated rule classifies a red border/text as an error indicator (vs decoration) or verifies a non-color error cue exists. aria-invalid presence (4.1.2/3.3.1) is a different, programmatic concern that explicitly does NOT satisfy 1.4.1's visible-alternative requirement — a distinction only a human applying the AT-decoupling note makes.

references.quote: A user submits an online form and leaves a required field blank, resulting in an error. The form field that caused the error is indicated by red text only, without an additional non-color indication that the field caused an error.
An error indicator cannot use color alone as an indicator.
An example of prompting a response would be: using highlighting on form fields to indicate that a required field had been left blank.

Conversely, even if information that is conveyed by color differences is appropriately conveyed to assistive technologies, it does not necessarily pass this criterion, as sighted users who cannot distinguish between certain color may not necessarily be using any assistive technologies. This criterion requires a visible alternative to color.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained forms that render the post-submit error state (pre-rendered on load, or via a small inline script triggered on submit). Vary the error cue: (1) red 2px border on invalid field vs gray same-lightness border on valid, no text; (2) invalid label text turns red, valid stays black, no message; (3) error summary that lists field names by re-coloring them red only; (4) inline-validation red outline that appears as you type, hint text unchanged; (5) red border PLUS aria-invalid='true' but no visible text — to test the AT-decoupling judgment (programmatic exposure does NOT rescue). Include TRUE-NEGATIVE pages: red border PLUS error text + warning icon, and a red error border at >3:1 lightness vs the valid gray border (passes via escape hatch).
suggestedScenarios: Login form that on submit gives the password field a red 2px border (valid fields keep a same-lightness gray border) with no inline error text.
Checkout form where invalid fields turn their label text red while valid labels stay black — no message, no icon — judged in post-submit state.
Error summary at top of form that lists failing fields ONLY by re-coloring matching field names red, with no textual 'error' word per field.
Inline-validation field that flashes a red outline while typing an invalid value, with the outline as the sole indicator (hint text below unchanged).
Field with a red error border PLUS aria-invalid='true' but no visible text/icon — fails 1.4.1 despite programmatic exposure (AT-decoupling).
TRUE-NEGATIVE: invalid fields get a red border PLUS an inline error message and a warning icon — should PASS.
TRUE-NEGATIVE: error border is red at >3:1 lightness vs the valid gray border (distinguishable in grayscale) — should PASS via the escape hatch.

aspects.title: Informational image/chart HAS a text alternative, but the alt restates the color RULE instead of resolving the color-encoded fact
aspects.description: An informational bitmap or inline SVG (bar chart, line graph, status dashboard, map) uses color to encode a categorical fact, and it HAS a text alternative — but the alt/caption restates the data values and the color rule ('red bars indicate sales below quota') rather than RESOLVING it (naming WHICH employees fell below quota). Because the alt is present and plausible, an automated checker sees a satisfied alt attribute and passes; only a human who reads the alt against the picture sees that the color-borne distinction is never spelled out in text. This is the canonical F13 failure — 'alt exists but under-describes the color-encoded info'. It requires reading the chart pixels, reading the prose, and comparing meaning.
aspects.scLimb: conveying information (LIMB 1) in non-text content — F13
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases for 1.4.1. Even where ACT touches alt text (1.1.1), rules only check alt presence/non-emptiness, never whether the alt CONTENT captures a color-encoded distinction inside the bitmap. Distinguishing 'red = below quota, so Mary and Bob failed' (resolved in alt) from 'red bars indicate below-quota sales' (color rule merely restated, names omitted) requires reading the chart, reading the prose, and comparing their meaning — pure semantic judgment no checker performs.

references.quote: The red bars indicate sales that were below the yearly quota". This text alternative fails to provide the information which is conveyed by the color red in the image.
The alternative should indicate which people did not meet the sales quota rather than relying on color.
Check that the information conveyed by color differences is not included in the text alternative for the image.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained pages with an informational (or inline SVG drawn with colored rects) plus a text alternative. The alt/caption must give all the numbers and STATE the color rule but OMIT the resolved fact (which entities are in the colored category). The evaluator must read the rendered chart to identify which bars/lines/regions are the salient color, then confirm the alt never names them. Include a TRUE-NEGATIVE page where the alt fully resolves the fact ('Bob and Fred fell below quota') so the color is redundant. Vary chart type (bar, line, pie, map, dashboard) so the visual-reading task differs per page.
suggestedScenarios: Bar chart of four employees' sales; alt lists all four numbers and says 'bars in red are below quota' but never names which employees are red/below.
Inline SVG pie chart where wedge-to-category mapping lives only in color-matched legend swatches with no labels; caption lists totals but can't be tied to wedges.
Weather map with alt 'Areas in red are under a severe heat warning' — no county names given; warned counties readable only by red fill.
Line graph image, alt 'green line is revenue, red line is cost'; the lines cross and the alt never states which is on top in any month.
Status dashboard screenshot, alt 'servers in green are healthy, red are down', lists server names but never says which are down.
TRUE-NEGATIVE: same bar chart but alt resolves the fact — 'Bob and Fred fell below quota; Mary and Andrew met it' — color is redundant, should PASS.

aspects.title: Color-coded charts, maps, diagrams and game pieces distinguished by color with no pattern, icon, or in-graphic label (G111)
aspects.description: Non-text graphics rely on solid color to distinguish categories — transit-map routes by color only, a bar/area chart whose series are told apart only by fill color matched to a color-only legend, a flow chart using green-background = pass / red-background = fail with no shape/label difference, an SVG diagram whose elements are identified by color with no number/legend pairing, or game pieces distinguished by color alone. Per G111 the fix is to ADD a pattern (hatching, dots, dashes), a distinct icon/shape, or an in-graphic text/number label so the same information survives without color. An evaluator must read the graphic, identify each color-coded category, and confirm no non-color visual encoding redundantly carries the same distinction. This differs from the F13-alt aspect: here the question is the in-graphic VISUAL encoding (pattern/shape), not whether a sibling alt text resolves it.
aspects.scLimb: distinguishing a visual element (LIMB 4) in non-text content — G111 (the 'and pattern' technique)
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases for 1.4.1. No automated checker can render a chart/map/diagram, segment its color regions, and decide whether each color-coded category ALSO carries a pattern, icon, shape, or in-graphic label. Recognizing that a transit-line color or a chart-series fill is the SOLE distinguishing cue — and that the legend itself is color-keyed — is a visual-semantic judgment.

references.quote: The objective of this technique is to ensure that when color differences are used to convey information within non-text content, patterns are included to convey the same information in a manner that does not depend on color.

An on-line map of a transportation system displays each route in a different color. The stops on each route are marked with a distinctive icon such as a diamond, square, or circle to help differentiate each route.
Check that all information that is conveyed using color is also conveyed using patterns that do not rely on color.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained pages with inline SVG (or canvas-style HTML) graphics where categories are color-only. Vary the graphic type: transit map with same-shape stations on differently-colored lines; multi-series bar/area chart with color-only legend; pass/fail flow chart by background color only; SVG chemistry-style diagram with color-only element identification; a board-game state with color-only pieces. Include TRUE-NEGATIVE pages that ADD the non-color encoding per G111: routes with diamond/square/circle station icons, chart series with distinct hatch patterns, the SVG examination example where each element has a number + legend. The grayscale technique is the canonical detection method — converting to grayscale should make failing graphics ambiguous and passing ones still readable.
suggestedScenarios: Inline-SVG transit map with three routes distinguished only by line color; all stations are identical dots — no icons/shapes/labels.
Multi-series area chart where the only series differentiator is fill color, matched to a swatch-only legend with no patterns.
Flow chart using green-background boxes for 'pass' branches and red-background boxes for 'fail' branches, identical shape and no label.
SVG molecule diagram where each chemical element is shown only by a colored circle, no number or in-image legend.
Color-coded conference schedule grid where each track is a different cell background color with no T1/T2/T3 text code.
TRUE-NEGATIVE: transit map where each route ALSO uses a distinct station icon (diamond/square/circle) per G111 — should PASS.
TRUE-NEGATIVE: SVG examination diagram where each element has BOTH a color AND a number with a color+number legend — should PASS.

aspects.title: UI buttons, controls, and color-coded categories signalling action/status by color with no text or character cue (G14)
aspects.description: Interactive UI conveys an action or a status by color alone with no redundant text/character cue: a green button = proceed / red button = cancel pair where the buttons are not labelled with distinguishing text and the only convention is 'green advances, red cancels'; a color that indicates a link opens in a new window or that a database entry updated successfully; color-coded list items, tabs, or schedule tracks distinguished only by background hue with no in-text code (T1/T2/T3). Per G14 the information conveyed by color differences must ALSO be conveyed explicitly in text (and per G205 the cue must be in the control's programmatic name). An evaluator must identify the action/status the color encodes, then confirm a non-color text/character cue redundantly carries it. This covers the 'indicating an action' limb that the link and form aspects do not.
aspects.scLimb: indicating an action (LIMB 2) and conveying status — G14 / G205 (green Go / red Cancel; color-coded tracks; new-window/updated indicators)
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases for 1.4.1. No automated checker can determine that a green-vs-red button pair encodes 'proceed vs cancel' purely by color, or that a category's background hue is the sole carrier of its track/status, and then verify a redundant text cue exists. Mapping a color to its intended action/status meaning and judging whether a text alternative carries the same information is contextual semantic reasoning.

references.quote: An on-line loan application explains that green buttons advance in the process and red buttons cancel the process.

The objective of this technique is to ensure that when color differences are used to convey information, such as required form fields, the information conveyed by the color differences are also conveyed explicitly in text.
Examples of indications of an action include: using color to indicate that a link will open in a new window or that a database entry has been updated successfully.
The text cue must be included as part of the programmatically determinable name for the control.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained pages where an action/status is encoded by color. Vary the mechanism: a pair of identically-shaped buttons distinguished only by green vs red fill with the convention stated only in prose; a list of links where 'opens in new window' is shown only by link color; a 'saved' confirmation conveyed only by a row turning green; color-coded schedule/tab categories by background hue with no text code. Include TRUE-NEGATIVE pages per G14/G205: green button labelled 'Go' and red labelled 'Cancel'; color-coded tracks with a T1/T2/T3 text code after each session name; a status row that turns green AND shows the word 'Saved'. The grayscale check should make failing pages ambiguous about which action/status is which.
suggestedScenarios: Two same-shaped, same-text-less submit buttons distinguished only by green vs red fill, with 'green proceeds, red cancels' stated only in body prose.
List of links where those opening in a new window are shown only by a different link color, with no icon or '(opens in new window)' text.
A 'record updated' confirmation conveyed only by the affected table row turning green, no 'Updated' / checkmark text.
Color-coded conference schedule where each track's sessions share a background hue with no T1/T2/T3 text code (G14 failing variant).
A toggle whose on/off state is shown only by green vs gray fill at <3:1 lightness, no ON/OFF text or position cue.
TRUE-NEGATIVE: green button labelled 'Go' and red button labelled 'Cancel' with instructions naming the labels (G14) — should PASS.
TRUE-NEGATIVE: color-coded schedule where each session also has a 'T1'/'T2'/'T3' text code after its name (G14) — should PASS.

aspects.title: Scoping boundary cases: 3:1-lightness pass, pure-color reliance fails regardless of contrast, non-applicability, and visited-link exemption
aspects.description: 1.4.1 has several boundary rules that produce PASS/NOT-APPLICABLE verdicts an over-eager evaluator (or a naive 'any color cue fails' heuristic) would get wrong, and one that produces a FAIL a contrast-only check would miss. (a) 3:1 LIGHTNESS ESCAPE HATCH: colors differing in lightness with a >=3:1 contrast ratio between them count as an additional visual distinction and PASS — the evaluator must compute the inter-element lightness ratio, not reflexively fail. (b) PURE-COLOR RELIANCE STILL FAILS regardless of contrast: if meaning depends on perceiving a particular hue (green outline = valid vs red = invalid), an additional indicator is required EVEN IF the two colors have high contrast with each other. (c) NON-APPLICABILITY: where color conveys NO information (a hyperlink styled identically to surrounding static text), 1.4.1 does not apply and there is no failure. (d) VISITED-LINK EXEMPTION: color-alone distinction of visited vs unvisited links does NOT fail, even below 3:1. Each requires applying a specific WCAG rule rather than a blanket judgment.
aspects.scLimb: all four limbs via the scoping notes: 3:1 lightness escape hatch; pure-color reliance regardless of contrast; non-applicability when color conveys nothing; visited-link exemption
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases for 1.4.1, so none of these boundaries is exercised. They are precisely the cases where naive automation goes wrong: a tool that flags any color cue would false-positive on the 3:1-lightness pass, the non-applicable identical-link, and the visited-link case; while the 'high contrast between two hues still fails if meaning depends on the hue' rule (green-valid vs red-invalid) is a subtlety no contrast checker models. Each demands applying a specific WCAG rule with human judgment about whether color is carrying meaning and which exemption governs.

references.quote: If content is conveyed through the use of colors that differ not only in their hue, but that also have a significant difference in lightness, then this counts as an additional visual distinction, as long as the difference in relative luminance between the colors leads to a contrast ratio of 3:1 or greater.

However, if content relies on the user's ability to accurately perceive or differentiate a particular color an additional visual indicator will be required regardless of the contrast ratio between those colors. For example, knowing whether an outline is green for valid or red for invalid.

a hyperlink which has been styled to appear no different than neighboring static text would not fail this success criterion, as there would be no color differentiation between the actionable hyperlink text and the adjacent static text.
Where color alone distinguishes between visited and unvisited links, it does not result in a failure of this Success Criterion, even where the contrast between the two link colors is below 3:1.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained pages that each isolate ONE boundary rule, mixing genuine passes/non-applicables with one true failure to force discrimination. For (a) build a page where status is shown by two hues that ALSO differ >=3:1 in lightness (light-green vs dark-red) — must PASS — paired conceptually with a same-lightness twin that fails. For (b) build a valid/invalid outline page where green and red have high mutual contrast but meaning depends on the hue — must FAIL despite the contrast. For (c) a page where an <a> is styled exactly like static text (no color difference) — NOT APPLICABLE / pass. For (d) a paragraph where visited links differ from unvisited by color only, below 3:1 — must PASS via the visited-link exemption. The evaluator must name which rule applies, not just pass/fail.
suggestedScenarios: Status shown by light-green vs dark-red text that also differ >=3:1 in lightness — should PASS via the lightness escape hatch (a naive 'color cue = fail' would wrongly flag it).
Same status concept but the two hues are at the SAME lightness (<3:1 between them) — should FAIL, the discriminating twin of the above.
Form field validity shown by a green outline (valid) vs red outline (invalid) where green/red have high mutual contrast but meaning depends on the hue — should FAIL regardless of contrast.
A hyperlink deliberately styled identical to surrounding static text (same color, no underline) — NOT APPLICABLE: no color conveys the link-ness, so no failure.
A paragraph where visited links are a different color from unvisited links only, with <3:1 between the two link colors — should PASS via the visited-link exemption.
An inverted-colors element (foreground/background swapped) with sufficient contrast used to distinguish a selected item — should PASS as an additional visual distinction.
A list where 'new' items are a different hue than 'old' items at the SAME lightness with no other cue — should FAIL, contrasted against a sibling list that adds a 'NEW' text tag (passes).

pages.scenario: Dark-mode coffee-industry editorial blog post. Four inline story links are brand blue #6f93cf with text-decoration:none and no weight/size/family/style change on near-white #e8e8ea body text over #0e0f12. Color-perceiving readers see blue; grayscale/color-blind readers cannot find the links.
pages.mechanism: Link #6f93cf vs body #e8e8ea is 2.54:1 lightness contrast (under the 3:1 escape hatch), so hue is the sole differentiator; no underline, weight, italic, size, or hover/focus cue. Link-vs-bg 6.16:1 and body-vs-bg 15.66:1 both pass 1.4.3, which is why contrast scanners stay silent.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no link-vs-surrounding-text contrast rule; they measure foreground-vs-background (1.4.3), which the link passes. Judging that 2.54:1 same-direction lightness is below 3:1 and hue is the only cue requires comparing link color to adjacent text color and applying the escape-hatch rule.

citation.quote: Removing the underline and leaving only the color difference for such links would be a failure because there would be no other visual indication (besides color) that it is a link.

pages.scenario: Fintech REST-API developer-docs glossary (<dl> of terms). In-definition cross-reference links (.xref) are a darker shade of the SAME neutral gray hue (#3d3d3d) as the mid-gray body (#6b6b6b), no underline, no weight/family change. Separate blue hover-underlined breadcrumb nav acts as a distractor.
pages.mechanism: Link #3d3d3d vs body #6b6b6b is 2.04:1 lightness and the same hue, so the only difference is a darkness step that does not reach the 3:1 G183/F73 same-hue threshold. Both grays pass 1.4.3 on white (10.86:1 / 5.33:1).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No fg-vs-bg violation exists (both grays clear 4.5:1 on white) so contrast rules are silent; no scanner compares a link color to adjacent text color, and none knows a 2:1 same-hue darkness step is too weak. Distinguishing real link spans from prose and judging sufficiency of the darkness step is perceptual.

citation.quote: Red and pink are the same color (hue) but they have different lightness (which is not color). So red and pink would pass the requirement for "not distinguished by color (hue) alone" since they differ by lightness (which is not color) - as long as the difference in lightness (contrast) is 3:1 or greater.

pages.scenario: Sourdough-focaccia recipe blog using the literal F73 stylesheet pattern: a:link/a:visited/a:active have text-decoration:none (resting green #1f6f43), and only a:hover (plus a:active) add an underline and red color. No :focus rule, so keyboard users also get color-only at rest.
pages.mechanism: In the resting state the only link-vs-text difference is hue (green vs near-black #2b2b2b) at 2.30:1 lightness, below 3:1. The underline/red cue exists in CSS and fires on mouseover but appears only on :hover/:active, and F73/G183 judge conformance before focus or pointing, so the hover-only cue does not rescue the color-only resting state.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Static scanners parse the resting computed style, see a 1.4.3-passing colored named <a>, and do not simulate :hover/:active or compare resting-vs-hover renders; they have no rule that hover-only cues fail. Catching this needs capturing resting+hover states and applying the F73 still-a-failure rule.

pages.scenario: City government 'Renew your resident parking permit' service page. Inline guidance links inside an ordered step list are gov-blue #2453a6 at rest (no underline, weight 400); the only non-color cue, font-weight:700, is injected via :focus-visible, so it appears only for keyboard users on focus. Mouse/touch/scanning and color-blind users get color-only.
pages.mechanism: Resting link #2453a6 vs body #1b1b1b is 2.35:1 lightness (under 3:1), hue is the sole differentiator; the bold cue requires :focus-visible to appear. F73 states a non-color cue provided only on focus is still a failure. A focus outline satisfies 2.4.7 but not 1.4.1's resting-state visual distinction. Colors pass 1.4.3 (6.96:1 / 16.34:1).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Scanners evaluate the 1.4.3-passing resting style, have no link-vs-text rule, and see a present :focus-visible style plus focus outline that superficially looks accessible. Recognizing the bold cue is keyboard-focus-gated and irrelevant to 1.4.1's resting requirement needs resting-vs-focused comparison and F73 knowledge.

citation.quote: If the non-color cue only happens when the mouse hovers over the link or when the link receives focus, it is still a failure.

pages.scenario: University LMS course page (HIST 214). The theme styles BOTH inline links (<a>) and lecturer emphasis (<strong>) with the identical maroon #9d1b3d + bold + no underline, so 'maroon+bold' is not a link-specific cue; half the maroon-bold phrases are reading-list links and half are non-link emphasis. Only the href reveals which are clickable.
pages.mechanism: The bold weight is real but shared with non-links, so it cannot signal link-ness, leaving color as the only link cue — and color cannot disambiguate links from identically-colored emphasis. Accent-vs-body is 2.01:1 (hue-dominant, under 3:1). Color-blind/grayscale users see uniform bold prose; sighted users must hover or read source. The link is not visually evident as a link.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <a> and <strong> are valid and 1.4.3-passing (7.90:1 on white); a scanner sees 'links are bold and colored' and would deem it sufficient, unable to know identical styling is reused for non-links or that a shared cue fails to distinguish links. Determining which colored-bold spans are links vs decorative emphasis requires reading meaning and markup.

citation.quote: While some links may be visually evident from page design and context, such as navigational links, links within text are often visually understood only from their own display attributes. Removing the underline and leaving only the color difference for such links would be a failure because there would be no other visual indication (besides color) that it is a link.

pages.mechanism: Link #3366CC vs black body text is 3.91:1 lightness contrast, at/above the 3:1 escape hatch, so links are distinguishable by lightness (not hue alone) even with no color perception or in grayscale. Correctly clearing the page requires computing the 3.91:1 link-vs-text lightness ratio and applying the 3:1 escape hatch — guarding against over-reporting.

pages.scenario: TRUE-NEGATIVE (INAPPLICABLE / non-applicability boundary). Bank Acceptable Use Policy. Three inline clause hyperlinks (.inline-ref) are styled identical to neighboring static text: same color #202124, same weight, no underline, no hover/focus change. Correctly classifying it as inapplicable requires recognizing link color equals body color (no color differentiation exists) and applying the Understanding note's non-applicability rule — distinguishing color-only differentiation that fails from no color differentiation at all.

pages.scenario: TRUE-NEGATIVE (long-tail RTL i18n): Arabic (dir=rtl, lang=ar) mobile-banking transfer form in the post-submit state. citation.quote: If content is conveyed through the use of colors that differ not only in their hue, but that also have a significant difference in lightness, then this counts as an additional visual distinction, as long as the difference in relative luminance between the colors leads to a contrast ratio of 3:1 or greater. For example, a light green and a dark red differ both by color (hue) and by lightness, so they would pass if the contrast ratio is at least 3:1.

No automated rule detects that two foreground hues at the same lightness are the sole carrier of a semantic category, nor that the colour legend fails to rescue colour-blind users. Recognising the green/red encodes spice level requires reading the menu's meaning and reasoning about colour perception.

citation.quote: Displaying content in grayscale may help identify content that uses only color to convey information.

pages.scenario: Reviewed job-application form where each field's validity is shown by outline colour only: light-green border = accepted, dark-red border = needs attention. The two outline colours have ~6.4:1 mutual contrast (well above 3:1), so the lightness gap is large, yet it still FAILS because the meaning depends on perceiving WHICH hue.
pages.mechanism: Field validity (accepted vs needs-attention) is communicated solely by border hue (green #86d98f vs dark red #7a1414). Per the Understanding note, when content relies on differentiating a particular colour an additional indicator is required REGARDLESS of the ~6.4:1 contrast between the colours. There is no check/alert icon, no 'Looks good'/'Required' text, no message, and no aria-invalid, so a red-green colour-blind user cannot tell which fields still need fixing.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Inputs are properly labelled, the 2px borders pass SC 1.4.11 non-text contrast, and the markup is valid, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse find no errors. No rule models 'the outline hue is the only thing distinguishing valid from invalid,' and the large >=3:1 inter-element contrast would actively mislead a tool or hasty human into thinking the lightness escape hatch applies. Catching it requires applying the pure-colour-reliance rule that hue-dependent meaning fails irrespective of contrast.

citation.quote: However, if content relies on the user's ability to accurately perceive or differentiate a particular color an additional visual indicator will be required regardless of the contrast ratio between those colors. For example, knowing whether an outline is green for valid or red for invalid.

pages.scenario: Government council cookie-and-tracking policy whose inline links are styled to look exactly like the surrounding static text (inherited colour, no underline at rest). Because colour is not used to distinguish the link from static text at all, SC 1.4.1 does not apply — there is no use-of-colour failure (NOT-APPLICABLE / pass).
pages.mechanism: For 1.4.1 the question is whether colour conveys information. The inline links inherit the body colour (#222) identical to the adjacent static text, so colour is not being used to distinguish the actionable link from the static text. The criterion's scope therefore excludes these links. This is distinct from F73, which fails when a link IS distinguished by colour but lacks a non-colour cue; here the link is not distinguished by colour at all.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive 'inline links should be underlined' or 'any link colour cue needs a backup' heuristic flags these links. Correctly classifying this requires recognising that colour conveys NOTHING here (link and text share one colour), which removes them from 1.4.1's scope — a scoping judgement no linter performs. The hover/focus underline further confuses a static scan, and distinguishing not-applicable from a genuine F73 failure is a human call.

citation.quote: This criterion does not apply to situations where color has not been used to convey information, indicate an action, prompt a response or distinguish a visual element. For instance, a hyperlink which has been styled to appear no different than neighboring static text would not fail this success criterion, as there would be no color differentiation between the actionable hyperlink text and the adjacent static text.

pages.scenario: Newsroom investigations archive where article links are underlined (distinguished from static text by a non-colour cue) and visited vs unvisited links differ by colour only, with ~1.09:1 contrast between the two link colours (below 3:1). PASSES via the visited-link exemption.
pages.mechanism: Links are distinguished from static text by an UNDERLINE (no F73 failure on the link-vs-text axis). The only colour-only distinction is visited (purple #5a3da8) vs unvisited (blue #1a52b5) at ~1.09:1, below 3:1. The Understanding note exempts colour-only visited/unvisited distinction even below 3:1, because the :visited pseudo-class is constrained to colour for privacy and conveying visited state is not an author responsibility. Both link colours still meet SC 1.4.3 against the page (~7:1).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A tool that measures :link vs :visited contrast and finds it below 3:1 might naively flag a use-of-colour or contrast problem. The correct verdict requires knowing the specific visited-link exemption — that conveying visited status is not an author responsibility because :visited is restricted to colour for privacy — which no checker encodes. Distinguishing this from a genuine F73 also requires confirming the underline carries the link-vs-text role.

citation.quote: Where color alone distinguishes between visited and unvisited links, it does not result in a failure of this Success Criterion, even where the contrast between the two link colors is below 3:1. Note that authors must continue to ensure that all text links meet contrast minimums against the page background (SC 1.4.3).

pages.scenario: Cinema showtime picker (radio-as-pills) where the chosen showtime is distinguished by inverting the pill's foreground and background (unselected dark-text-on-white; selected white-text-on-dark). The inversion is an additional visual distinction with ~15.7:1 lightness difference, so it PASSES.
pages.mechanism: The selected state reverses the pill's foreground and background colours rather than tinting it. This is not a hue cue: in greyscale the selected pill is a DARK block among LIGHT blocks, differing from the unselected fills by ~15.7:1 in lightness, so it is unmistakable without colour perception. The Understanding note states inversion passes 1.4.1 given sufficient contrast. Selection is also exposed via the native radio's checked state.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: An over-eager 'selected state shown by a colour change = use-of-colour failure' heuristic (the classic swatch/chip anti-pattern that audit tools and naive LLMs flag) false-positives on this pill. Distinguishing a genuine colour-only state cue from an INVERSION carrying an inherent large lightness difference requires comparing the selected and unselected fills and luminances and reasoning that the swap survives greyscale — a visual judgement no checker makes.

citation.quote: Similarly, if content is distinguished by inverting an element's foreground and background colors, this would pass (again, assuming that the foreground and background colors have a sufficient contrast).

pages.scenario: Cloud-platform status console with a 'Region health' matrix where each region/service state (operational/degraded/major outage) is shown only by the hue of an identically-shaped green/amber/red dot. Meaning depends on perceiving the specific hue, so it FAILS; a sibling 'Active incidents' list that adds text badges is the passing contrast.
pages.mechanism: Each health value is encoded only in dot hue (green #3fbf63 / amber #e0a02e / red #e0503e), with identical shape and size and no text/pattern. The dots have ample non-text contrast vs the dark surface (4.8-8.3:1), so this is not a 1.4.11 issue, and the hues are at similar lightness (green/amber ~1.04:1), so no escape hatch applies. Per the Understanding note, reliance on perceiving a particular colour requires an additional indicator regardless of contrast. The legend only re-encodes colour; a colour-blind operator sees a grid of identical dark dots.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The dots are well-formed elements with sufficient non-text contrast, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse find no error. No rule can tell that a coloured dot ENCODES a status available through no other channel, that the legend doesn't rescue colour-blind users, or that the adjacent text-badge incidents list doesn't cover the matrix. Recognising hue is the sole carrier of 'operational vs degraded vs down' — and that it fails regardless of the dots' contrast — is a semantic/visual judgement.

citation.quote: However, if content relies on the user's ability to accurately perceive or differentiate a particular color an additional visual indicator will be required regardless of the contrast ratio between those colors.
